title: When I was a kid
goals: Say where and when you were born and grew up, using was / were born.
Talk about your childhood with the past simple: positive sentences, negative sentences and questions.
Put events in time with ago, for, from… to, until, when, in and last.
Talk about how many people or things with all, most, a few, some, none (of).
Name school subjects and talk about your life as a student.
Correct yourself when you speak with Well, Actually, No, wait and I mean, and contrast with except (for) and apart from.

learn.title: was / were born
learn.html:
To say where or when you were born, we use the past of be with born. You do not use a special verb for «born»: say I was born.

SubjectPositiveNegative
I / he / she / itI was born in Puebla.She wasn't born in Mexico.
you / we / theyMy parents were born in Oaxaca.We weren't born in 1990.
QuestionShort answer
Were you born in Mexico City?Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.
Was your sister born here?Yes, she was. / No, she wasn't.
Where were you born?I was born in Toluca.
When was he born?He was born in 1987.

With places, use in (in Puebla). With years, also use in (in 1995). With a full date, use on: on May 5th.

watch.why: Born always comes after was / were.
In a question with born, use was / were, not did.

watch.wrong: My parents was born in Oaxaca.
watch.right: My parents were born in Oaxaca.

watch.why: Birth is in the past: use was.

learn.title: Past simple (review): regular and irregular verbs
learn.html:
We use the past simple for actions that finished in the past. The form is the same for all subjects (I lived, she lived, they lived).

TypeRuleExamples
Regular verbs+ -ed (if the verb ends in e, add only + d)live → lived, move → moved, play → played
Consonant + yy → i + -edstudy → studied, cry → cried
One syllable CVCdouble the consonantstop → stopped
Irregular verbsthey change; you must memorize themgo → went, grow up → grew up, leave → left, come → came, speak → spoke, have → had, get → got, take → took
NegativeQuestionShort answer
I didn't live there long.Did you live there long?Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
We didn't leave until 1997.Where did you grow up?I grew up in Monterrey.

With didn't and did, the verb goes back to its base form: I didn't go, Did you go?

watch.why: After didn't, use the base form.

watch.wrong: Did you moved to another city?
watch.right: Did you move to another city?
watch.why: After did, use the base form.
In questions with normal verbs, you need did.

learn.title: Time expressions: ago, for, from… to, until, when
learn.html:
These words place an action in the past.

WordMeaningExample
last + year / month / week / daythe previous oneShe moved here last May.
in + month / yearinI started school in 2005.
for + periodduringWe lived there for six years.
period + agoago (before now)I came here three years ago.
from… tofrom… to (start and end)He studied there from 1995 to 2001.
until + year / sentenceuntilWe stayed until 1997. I lived there until I was six.
when + sentencewhenI moved when I was ten.
thenthen, after thatWe left Puebla. Then we came to Mexico City.

We read years in two parts: 1988 = nineteen eighty-eight; 2007 = two thousand (and) seven; 2015 = twenty fifteen.

watch.wrong: I lived there since three years.
watch.right: I lived there for three years.
watch.why: A length of time in the past uses for.

watch.wrong: I moved here before three years.
watch.right: I moved here three years ago.
watch.why: «Ago» comes after the time period: three years ago.
Do not use in with last.

watch.wrong: I lived there until five years old.
watch.right: I lived there until I was five.

learn.title: all, most, some, a few, no / none (of)
learn.html:
These words say how many. They change depending on whether you speak in general or about specific people.

MeaningStructureExample
General (people in general)word + noun, no ofMost people study English. A few students take Latin. No students like exams.
Specific (the / my / these)word + of + the / my…Most of my friends know French. None of my classmates failed.
With a pronounword + of + them / usAll of them passed. Some of us went.
  • Order from most to least: all (everyone) > most (the majority) > a lot of / some (many) > a few (a small number) > none / no (nobody).
  • Before a noun, use no. Alone or before of, use none: No students came. None of the students came.
  • A lot of always takes of: A lot of people speak English.

watch.wrong: Most of people in my town drive.
watch.right: Most people in my town drive.
watch.why: In a general sense, do not use of.
Before of, use none, not «no of».
After of, use the object pronoun: them.

watch.right: Some of my classmates are bilingual.
watch.why: With my / the, you need of.

learn.title: Correcting yourself and contrasting
learn.html:
When you remember something, sometimes you make a mistake. In English you correct yourself with these expressions:

  • Well, … — to start remembering: Well, I remember my first day.
  • Actually, … — to correct or make something more exact: I was five. Actually, I was six.
  • No, wait. … — you realize you made a mistake: It was 1999… no, wait, it was 2000.
  • I mean, … — to correct a word or a name: My teacher, I mean, my coach, called my mom.

To connect ideas that contrast, use except (for) or apart from (except, other than):

  • We agreed on most things except (for) the car. = … apart from the car.
  • I didn't like my classes except for art.

checklist: At least three past verbs (one irregular)
A time expression: ago, for, until or from… to

I studied at a public school until I was eighteen. I liked math and art, but I didn't like history. Most of my teachers were kind. A few of my classmates were my best friends. reading.title: Between two countries
reading.intro: Read Daniela's text and answer the questions.
paragraphs: My name is Daniela, and I'm twenty-six. I was born in Los Angeles in 1999, but my parents are from Zacatecas. They moved to California in 1995 because there was more work there. My father worked in a restaurant for ten years, and my mother cleaned offices at night. We spoke Spanish at home, so I grew up bilingual. I still remember the smell of my grandmother's kitchen in Zacatecas.

When I was eight, we moved to Guadalajara. I didn't want to leave my close friends, and I cried on the plane. At first, school was difficult. I didn't understand some words in Spanish class, and I got into trouble once because I talked in English! But after a few months, I made new friends. Most of my classmates were kind, and all of them wanted to practice English with me.

My favorite subjects were art and choir. I didn't like algebra, but I loved drama. I stayed in Guadalajara until I was eighteen. Then I went to university in Monterrey, where I majored in economics. I got along with everybody there, except for one roommate. Last year I got a job in Mexico City. My boss asks me, "Where are you from?" and I say, "Well, actually, I'm from two places!"

listening.title: Old school photos
listening.intro: Listen to the conversation between Ben and Marisol. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Is this you in the photo, Marisol?
Yes, it is! That's my first day of school. I was five. No, wait... I was six.
I was born in Veracruz, but we moved to Mexico City when I was two.
Yes, I did. I had two close friends, Paty and Ana. We played together for ten years.
Art! Most of my classes were boring, but I loved art. I didn't like math at all.
Do you talk to Paty and Ana now?
Paty, yes. We talk every week. Ana moved to Canada three years ago, so I don't see her much.
That's sad. Did you learn English at school?
Only a few of us took English, but I studied it until I was eighteen.
